latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Total viable mycobacterial load disseminated across organs; central driver of all downstream organ-specific pathology and the variable that anti-TB chemotherapy reduces over weeks to months.
Active seeding of mycobacteria via bloodstream from primary or reactivation focus to multiple organs producing miliary pattern; typically follows breakdown of caseous focus into vascular structure.

Th1-driven epithelioid granuloma formation across lungs, liver, spleen, marrow, lymph nodes, meninges; underlies tissue dysfunction, miliary radiographic pattern, hepatosplenomegaly, and elevated ACE/ADA.
IL-12/IFN-γ-driven activation of macrophages; necessary for granuloma containment but also drives systemic constitutional symptoms (fever, anorexia, wasting) and CXCL9/CXCL10 elevation.
IL-6 driven hepatic acute phase reactant production (CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen) and suppression of negative APRs (albumin); also contributes to anemia of chronic inflammation via hepcidin.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Host immune compromise / cell-mediated immunity blunting
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Reduced T-cell and macrophage competence (HIV, anti-TNF, steroids, malnutrition, age); permits progression from latent to disseminated and produces TST/IGRA anergy in severe cases.
Diffuse 1–3 mm randomly distributed pulmonary granulomas producing alveolar–capillary barrier dysfunction, restrictive physiology, hypoxemia and (uncommonly) ARDS-spectrum injury.
Diffuse non-caseating to caseating hepatic granulomas; produces cholestatic liver enzyme pattern (ALP/GGT > AST/ALT), hepatomegaly, hyperbilirubinemia, and hypoalbuminemia.

Granulomatous infiltration of marrow with cytokine-mediated suppression of hematopoiesis; produces variable cytopenias including pancytopenia, leukoerythroblastic blood film, and high-yield AFB on marrow biopsy.

Rich-focus rupture into subarachnoid space producing basilar exudative meningitis, vasculitis of perforating arteries, hydrocephalus, and cranial neuropathies; the dominant driver of mortality and long-term disability in disseminated TB.

Bilateral adrenal involvement (TB is the historical leading cause of Addison disease); progressive cortical destruction produces primary adrenal insufficiency with hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypotension, hyperpigmentation.
TB is a recognized infectious trigger for secondary HLH/MAS; dysregulated macrophage activation produces hyperferritinemia, hypofibrinogenemia, hypertriglyceridemia, cytopenias, and very high sIL-2R.
TNF-α and IL-6 driven loss of lean mass with anorexia, night sweats, sustained weight loss; classic 'consumption' phenotype; reverses slowly with effective therapy.

Idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury from isoniazid and pyrazinamide (rifampin contributes mainly to cholestasis); produces ALT/AST rise typically in weeks 2–8 of therapy; superimposed on TB hepatic granulomas, requires careful attribution.

Worsening of TB lesions or new lesions despite microbiological response, driven by recovering immune response (often after ART initiation in HIV); presents weeks 2–12 of therapy with new fevers, expanding nodes, worsening CNS or pulmonary disease.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Loss of cell-mediated immunity (HIV with low CD4, anti-TNF, steroids, malnutrition, age extremes) permits unchecked mycobacterial replication and progression from latent or limited infection to disseminated disease.
Erosion of caseating focus into vasculature releases mycobacteria into bloodstream; magnitude of burden determines size and persistence of bacillemia and extent of organ seeding.
Seeded mycobacteria recruit Th1 lymphocytes and macrophages at every implant site, producing the multi-organ granulomatous picture characteristic of miliary TB.

Mycobacterial antigen-driven IL-12 production from macrophages activates Th1 lymphocytes to release IFN-γ; this cytokine axis is necessary for granuloma maintenance and produces systemic constitutional features.
IFN-γ and TNF-α activate macrophages to produce IL-6, the dominant driver of hepatic acute phase reactant transcription.
IFN-γ, IL-6, and TNF-α are pyrogenic; classical TB fever is low-grade evening rise with night sweats but disseminated TB often shows hectic, persistent high fevers reaching 39–40°C.
IL-6 is the dominant transcriptional driver of hepatic CRP; CRP is moderately elevated in disseminated TB though typically less than in pyogenic sepsis.
Fibrinogen and immunoglobulin elevation under IL-6 drive raise ESR substantially in chronic granulomatous infections; ESR > 100 mm/h is common in disseminated TB.
IL-6 induces hepcidin and ferritin transcription, raising serum ferritin; very high values (>10,000 ng/mL) suggest superimposed macrophage activation rather than acute phase alone.
Albumin is a negative acute phase reactant; chronic IL-6 drive plus malnutrition produces hypoalbuminemia commonly < 3.0 g/dL in disseminated TB.
Hepcidin-mediated iron sequestration and chronic inflammation produce normocytic anemia of chronic disease; further compounded by marrow involvement.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Effect is small relative to bacterial sepsis; PCT is typically only mildly elevated or normal in disseminated TB and useful for ruling out concurrent pyogenic infection.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mycobacterial intracellular biology produces less PCT induction than gram-negative bacteremia; persistently low PCT in a febrile septic-appearing patient should prompt consideration of TB and other intracellular pathogens.
Hematogenous seeding of pulmonary capillaries produces randomly distributed 1–3 mm nodules of granulomatous inflammation, the radiographic miliary pattern.
Pulmonary miliary disease produces diffuse fine random nodules visible on chest CT before plain radiograph; CT sensitivity is much higher than CXR especially in early dissemination.
Diffuse alveolar-interstitial granulomatous disease impairs gas exchange producing hypoxemia, which is exertional early and can become severe in extensive miliary disease.
Hypoxemia and reduced lung compliance from diffuse interstitial granulomas drive tachypnea, often the earliest objective respiratory sign before frank desaturation.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk highest in extensive miliary disease, severely immunocompromised hosts, and when paradoxical reactions develop early in therapy.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Extensive pulmonary involvement and host inflammatory response can progress to acute respiratory failure with diffuse alveolar damage pattern (miliary TB-associated ARDS).
Hepatic involvement is the most consistent extrapulmonary feature of disseminated TB; liver biopsy shows granulomas with high diagnostic yield.
Granulomatous infiltration enlarges the liver; tender hepatomegaly is a common bedside finding in disseminated TB.

TB hepatic involvement classically produces a cholestatic pattern with ALP and GGT elevation predominating over moderate transaminase rise; an isolated very elevated ALP in a febrile wasted patient should prompt evaluation for hepatic TB.

Mild to moderate transaminase elevation is common (typically 1–5× ULN); marked transaminitis in a patient already on therapy should raise concern for drug-induced liver injury rather than disease progression.
Hepatic granulomatous inflammation produces modest AST elevation; pattern with AST > ALT may also reflect malnutrition and concurrent alcohol use disorder common in this population.
Granulomatous biliary obstruction or extensive parenchymal involvement produces conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a subset; severe jaundice is a poor prognostic feature.
Hematogenous seeding of marrow produces granulomas with high AFB yield; bone marrow biopsy with culture is a high-yield invasive diagnostic test in occult disseminated TB.
Marrow infiltration combined with anemia of chronic disease produces variable anemia; severe anemia or pancytopenia raises concern for HLH/MAS overlay.
Marrow involvement and inflammatory cytokine suppression of megakaryopoiesis produce thrombocytopenia; severe thrombocytopenia (<50) is uncommon without superimposed HLH or DIC.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: WBC may instead be normal or mildly elevated; leukoerythroblastic blood film with circulating immature myeloid and nucleated red cells is a classic feature of marrow infiltration.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Marrow replacement and cytokine suppression produce variable cytopenias; pancytopenia with leukoerythroblastic picture in a febrile wasted patient should prompt evaluation for disseminated TB.
Splenic granulomatous infiltration with reactive hyperplasia produces splenomegaly, often palpable; combined with hepatomegaly forms hepatosplenomegaly characteristic of disseminated TB.
Multi-station lymph node enlargement (mediastinal, abdominal, cervical) is common; enlarged necrotic mediastinal nodes on CT support extrapulmonary spread.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk is concentrated in young children, HIV-infected patients, and those with high mycobacterial burden; CNS involvement complicates 10–30% of disseminated TB.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Hematogenous seeding produces subependymal Rich foci that can rupture into CSF and trigger basilar exudative meningitis with hydrocephalus and stroke from vasculitis.
Hydrocephalus, basilar inflammation, and ischemic strokes from vasculitis produce subacute confusion, decreased GCS, cranial nerve palsies; presentation may be insidious over weeks.
Subacute meningitis presents with headache, often progressive over 1–3 weeks before frank neurological signs; meningismus may be subtle or absent.

TBM is a defining complication of disseminated TB and the dominant driver of mortality and long-term neurologic disability; British Medical Research Council stage 2–3 carries high mortality even with treatment.

Bilateral adrenal involvement is common at autopsy in disseminated TB and is the historical leading cause of primary adrenal insufficiency worldwide; clinically apparent adrenal crisis is much rarer than radiographic enlargement.
Cortisol and aldosterone deficiency produce hypotension that can be refractory to fluids and pressors without hydrocortisone replacement.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Hyponatremia in disseminated TB is multifactorial: SIADH from CNS or pulmonary disease, adrenal insufficiency, and salt-losing nephropathy may all contribute.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency produce hyponatremia, often with hyperkalemia; hyponatremia is one of the most common electrolyte derangements in disseminated TB.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk is amplified by rifampin (CYP3A4 induction further reduces residual cortisol) and by stress of intercurrent illness.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Decompensation with shock, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, hypoglycemia in a patient with disseminated TB should prompt empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone.
Cytokine-mediated anorexia and lean mass loss produce sustained progressive weight loss often >10% body weight, a defining feature of consumption.
Drenching night sweats reflect resolution of evening fevers; classical TB constitutional symptom present in most disseminated cases.
Profound fatigue and anorexia accompany sustained cytokine activation and cachexia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Smear sensitivity is poor in extrapulmonary and paucibacillary disease; sputum smear may be negative even in disseminated TB if pulmonary involvement is purely interstitial-miliary.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Smear detects burdens above ~10^4 organisms/mL; useful for high-burden cavitary cases but insensitive in miliary or extrapulmonary disease.
Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra are the recommended initial tests; Ultra is sensitive in paucibacillary CSF and tissue and provides rifampin resistance result; positivity correlates with burden.
Liquid culture (MGIT) remains the gold standard; sensitive to lower burdens than smear and required for full drug-susceptibility testing; long turnaround means it does not drive initial therapy.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Anergy is most common in HIV with low CD4, severe malnutrition, and miliary TB itself; a negative TST/IGRA in a febrile wasted patient does not exclude disseminated TB.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Up to 25–50% of patients with disseminated/miliary TB are TST-negative due to anergy; IGRA is similarly impaired in severe disease and immunocompromise.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Applies when CNS involvement is present; CSF ADA > 10 U/L raises pre-test probability of TBM in the right epidemiologic context but is not specific.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Adenosine deaminase from activated lymphocytes is elevated in tuberculous compartmental inflammation (CSF, pleural, peritoneal); supports diagnosis of TBM, TB pleuritis, TB peritonitis.
Yellow-white choroidal granulomas on dilated fundoscopy are essentially pathognomonic for miliary TB and should prompt formal ophthalmologic exam in any febrile wasted patient with negative work-up.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Triggered most often in highly immunocompromised hosts (HIV, transplant, primary immunodeficiency); can also occur in immunocompetent miliary TB and may dominate the clinical picture.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: TB is a classical infectious trigger for secondary HLH; persistent antigenic stimulation and impaired cytotoxic clearance produce hyperinflammatory macrophage activation.
Ferritin > 10,000 ng/mL is highly suggestive of HLH overlay; values 1000–10,000 may reflect either severe acute phase response or developing macrophage activation.
sIL-2R reflects T-cell activation; elevation alongside hyperferritinemia, cytopenias, hypofibrinogenemia, and hypertriglyceridemia supports HLH.
Progression from subclinical activation to full HLH carries very high mortality; treatment focuses on aggressive anti-TB therapy with selective use of immunosuppression.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Develops in 5–20% receiving RIPE; risk amplified by age, alcohol use, viral hepatitis carriage, slow acetylator status for INH, malnutrition.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury from INH and PZA produces ALT > 3× ULN with symptoms or > 5× ULN asymptomatic, prompting drug withdrawal and rechallenge protocol.
Severe DILI with jaundice and synthetic dysfunction is uncommon but life-threatening and requires immediate stop of all hepatotoxic agents.
Drug-induced fulminant hepatitis is a recognized serious adverse event; fatality is uncommon but rises sharply with continued exposure after symptoms or AST/ALT > 5× ULN.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Highest risk in HIV with low CD4 starting ART within 2–8 weeks of TB therapy and in patients with high TB burden.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Recovering immune function reacts against residual antigens producing worsening fever, lymphadenitis, CNS deterioration, or new pulmonary infiltrates; can be life-threatening for CNS-IRIS.
Untreated disseminated TB approaches universal mortality; even with treatment, in-hospital mortality is 15–30% and higher in TBM, HIV, late initiation, and HLH overlay.
TBM carries the highest mortality of all TB syndromes (20–50% even with treatment, higher in advanced BMRC stage and HIV).
TB-associated HLH carries reported mortality of 50% or higher; early recognition and prompt anti-TB therapy are essential.
TB-associated ARDS carries very high mortality, particularly when paradoxical worsening occurs early in treatment.
Fulminant DILI requires drug interruption and increases overall mortality both directly and by delaying effective TB therapy.
The disease can present with persistent or recurrent fever over the observed clinical history.
Ordinary antibacterial regimens do not treat disseminated TB; pulmonary disease drives cough and dyspnea.
Pulmonary, cardiac, serosal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement can cause dyspnea.
Pulmonary or airway involvement can cause cough.

axes.shape_free_text: Insidious low-grade fever progressing to sustained fevers 38.5–40°C with classical evening rise and night sweats; may be hectic in HLH overlay; defervescence with effective therapy typically over 7–21 days but can be slower.
Sustained sinus tachycardia tracking fever and systemic illness; relative bradycardia is uncommon in TB.
Tachypnea proportional to extent of pulmonary miliary involvement; can rise sharply in TB-ARDS.
Ranges from normal at rest in mild miliary disease to severe hypoxemia in extensive disease or ARDS; exertional desaturation is an early sign.
Usually preserved; falls in adrenal crisis or HLH/septic-physiology overlay; refractory hypotension in disseminated TB should prompt evaluation for adrenal insufficiency.
Sustained weight loss over weeks to months, often cumulatively > 10% baseline body weight; hallmark of consumption.
Profound progressive fatigue, often severe enough to limit ADLs; gradually improves over months on therapy.
Drenching nocturnal sweats requiring change of clothes/linens; classical TB constitutional feature, resolves within weeks of effective therapy.
Dry or productive cough as a symptom axis; mechanism depends on pulmonary, airway, cardiac, or mediastinal involvement.
Subacute progressive headache over 1–3 weeks signals CNS involvement; persistent headache in any febrile disseminated TB patient warrants LP.
Subacute confusion, lethargy, decreased GCS in TBM; may also reflect adrenal crisis with hyponatremia or HLH.
Progressive enlargement of liver from granulomatous infiltration; resolves slowly with treatment over months.
Variable splenic enlargement; very large spleen is unusual and suggests HLH overlay or alternative diagnosis.
Multi-station nodal enlargement (cervical, axillary, mediastinal, abdominal); biopsy yield is high; nodes can paradoxically enlarge during IRIS.
axes.second_peak: Common during IRIS at weeks 2–12 of therapy

axes.shape_free_text: Yellow-white choroidal nodules on dilated fundoscopy; essentially pathognomonic for miliary TB; present in 15–30% of cases when sought.
Often normal or mildly low; leukoerythroblastic blood film with marrow involvement; marked leukocytosis suggests concurrent pyogenic infection.
Variable; mild neutropenia common with marrow involvement; severe neutropenia raises concern for HLH.
Normocytic anemia of chronic disease (typically 8–11 g/dL); slow recovery over months on therapy.
Reactive thrombocytosis common; thrombocytopenia indicates marrow involvement or HLH overlay.
Mild to moderate transaminase elevation (1–5× ULN) baseline from granulomatous hepatitis; second peak at 2–8 weeks of therapy from drug-induced liver injury is common and clinically critical.
axes.second_peak: DILI second peak at 14–60 days post-treatment start, can reach >5× ULN

axes.shape_free_text: Parallels ALT; AST > ALT may reflect malnutrition or alcohol use; sharp rise on therapy concerning for DILI.
Cholestatic-pattern ALP elevation predominates over transaminases in TB hepatic involvement; values commonly 2–5× ULN.
Mild conjugated hyperbilirubinemia in a subset; severe jaundice indicates either extensive hepatic TB or DILI and is a poor prognostic feature.
Reduced from chronic IL-6 drive plus malnutrition; slow recovery over months on effective therapy and nutrition.
Hyponatremia is one of the most common derangements; multifactorial (SIADH from CNS/pulmonary disease, adrenal insufficiency, salt-losing nephropathy).
Usually normal; may rise with renal TB, ATN from sepsis or hypovolemia, or adrenal crisis dehydration.
Elevated reflecting tissue turnover and hepatic involvement; very high values suggest HLH or alternative diagnosis (lymphoma).
Moderately elevated from acute phase response; values >10,000 ng/mL suggest superimposed macrophage activation/HLH.
Moderately elevated, typically 30–150 mg/L; lower than in pyogenic sepsis at comparable severity.
Substantially elevated, frequently > 100 mm/h; declines slowly over months on therapy; useful for follow-up trend.
Typically only mildly elevated (<2 ng/mL); persistently low PCT in severe sepsis-like illness should raise consideration of mycobacterial or viral etiology.
Elevated reflecting T-cell activation; very high (>2400 U/mL) supports HLH overlay; can be used to monitor immune activation.
IFN-γ-induced chemokine; elevated in disseminated TB and very elevated in HLH.
Often negative on sputum in pure miliary disease; smear from extrapulmonary specimens (BAL, marrow, lymph node) raises yield; quantitative grading correlates with burden.
Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra positivity from sputum, BAL, CSF, tissue, blood; sensitivity highest in pulmonary and tissue samples; provides rapid rifampin resistance result.
Liquid culture (MGIT) gold standard, time to positivity 1–6 weeks; remains positive for weeks despite therapy; required for drug-susceptibility testing.
Sensitivity reduced (anergy) in disseminated disease, especially in HIV, malnutrition, severe illness; negative result does not rule out disease.
Elevated CSF ADA (>10 U/L) supports TBM in compatible epidemiology; not specific.
Diffuse 1–3 mm random nodules on chest CT; CXR may be normal early but typically shows miliary pattern within weeks; HRCT is the most sensitive non-invasive test.
Low background; elevated in extensive miliary involvement, severely immunocompromised, paradoxical reactions; declines with effective therapy.
Elevated whenever disseminated TB is present, especially in young children, HIV, and high-burden disease; declines on effective therapy with adjunct dexamethasone.
Low absolute hazard but precipitable by intercurrent illness or rifampin-induced cortisol metabolism; high case-fatality if unrecognized.
Elevated in HIV, severely immunocompromised hosts, high mycobacterial burden; recognition triggers escalation of supportive care and consideration of immunomodulation.
Time-dependent hazard concentrated in weeks 2–8 of RIPE therapy; rises with age, pre-existing liver disease, alcohol use, malnutrition.
Elevated weeks 2–12 of effective therapy, particularly in HIV-coinfected patients starting ART within 2–8 weeks of TB therapy.

Untreated approaches universal mortality over weeks to months; treated in-hospital mortality 15–30% overall, higher in TBM, HIV with low CD4, late initiation, HLH overlay; declines steeply with effective therapy after 2–4 weeks.
History-level fever burden over days to months, distinct from a single measured body temperature.

axes.display_name: Lack of clinical response to standard antibacterial therapy
axes.shape_free_text: Persistent fever, inflammation, or organ findings despite antibacterial therapy that should have covered ordinary bacterial infection.
Patient-reported or observed breathlessness from pulmonary, cardiac, mediastinal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Fever-driven sinus tachycardia produces correlated daily noise on top of mechanism-driven trend.
Both share IL-6/acute phase axis as latent driver, but ESR responds slower than CRP, producing imperfect correlation.
Hepatocellular injury releases both enzymes in parallel; AST/ALT ratio shifts modestly with etiology (DILI, alcoholic injury, granulomatous hepatitis).
Transition to clinical TBM markedly raises mortality; advanced BMRC stage at presentation has 30–50% mortality.
TB-ARDS carries very high case-fatality, particularly when triggered by paradoxical reactions or in advanced disease.
TB-associated HLH carries reported mortality of 50% or more.
Severe DILI requires drug interruption, raising both direct hepatic mortality and indirect mortality through delayed effective TB therapy.
Unrecognized adrenal crisis with refractory shock has high case-fatality; promptly reversible with hydrocortisone.
CNS-IRIS and severe pulmonary IRIS contribute to mortality despite microbiologically effective therapy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: INH is the dominant cause of anti-TB DILI; risk amplified by age, alcohol, slow-acetylator status, viral hepatitis carriage.
Severe immunocompromise slows microbiological response; longer continuation phase often required.

side_effects.interpretation: Idiosyncratic hepatocellular injury, threshold for stop is symptoms with ALT>3×ULN or asymptomatic >5×ULN

treatments.context_specific_role: Cornerstone of intensive (2 months) and continuation (4–10 months) phases; must be combined with companion drugs to prevent resistance

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rifampin contributes more to cholestatic injury than to hepatocellular pattern.

failure_modes: Rifampin resistance (MDR-TB) — Xpert MTB/RIF detects rapidly
Severe drug interactions (CYP3A4 inducer) including with ART, anticoagulants, contraceptives
treatments.context_specific_role: Critical sterilizing agent; loss of rifampin (resistance, intolerance) markedly worsens outcomes and lengthens regimens to 18+ months

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: PZA contributes substantially to DILI risk especially in older adults; routinely held in pregnancy in some guidelines.

treatments.context_specific_role: Sterilizing activity in acidic intracellular environment; used in 2-month intensive phase; allows shortening of total therapy from 9 to 6 months in non-CNS disease

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Renally cleared; dose adjustment required to limit optic toxicity.

failure_modes: Optic neuritis / retrobulbar neuritis (red-green color vision loss)
Inadequate cidal activity if used as monotherapy

side_effects.interpretation: Dose-related optic neuritis; visual acuity and color discrimination should be monitored monthly

treatments.context_specific_role: Companion drug to prevent resistance during 2-month intensive phase, particularly while drug-susceptibility testing is pending
Routine adjunct to isoniazid (25–50 mg/day) to prevent peripheral neuropathy; particularly important in HIV, malnutrition, alcoholism, pregnancy, diabetes, renal failure

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Adjunctive dexamethasone reduces mortality in TBM (Thwaites trial), particularly in HIV-negative patients; standard taper over 6–8 weeks.
Steroids increase risk of opportunistic infections and hyperglycemia.

failure_modes: Tapering too rapidly leading to neurologic deterioration
treatments.context_specific_role: Standard adjunct in TBM and TB pericarditis; tapered over 6–8 weeks; benefit less established for non-CNS disseminated TB without specific complication

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Earlier ART initiation in low-CD4 HIV/TB co-infection lowers mortality but raises IRIS risk; standard timing is 2 weeks for CD4 < 50, 8 weeks otherwise (excluding TBM).

failure_modes: Drug interactions with rifampin (NNRTI levels reduced)

side_effects.interpretation: Paradoxical reaction with new fevers, lymphadenitis, neurologic worsening

treatments.context_specific_role: Co-treatment is essential in HIV/TB; rifampin requires regimen adjustment (efavirenz preferred, dolutegravir doubled, avoid PIs without rifabutin)

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Particularly relevant when combined with bedaquiline or clofazimine in MDR regimens.

failure_modes: QT prolongation, especially with companion agents
treatments.context_specific_role: Used for MDR-TB regimens, INH-intolerance, and as substitute for hepatotoxic drugs during DILI re-challenge

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Marrow toxicity is dose- and duration-dependent; in disseminated TB with marrow involvement, additive cytopenias can be problematic.

failure_modes: Peripheral and optic neuropathy with prolonged use
treatments.context_specific_role: Backbone of modern MDR/XDR regimens (BPaL, BPaLM); not first-line in drug-susceptible disease

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: QT prolongation, additive with fluoroquinolones and clofazimine.

failure_modes: Long terminal half-life leading to delayed adverse effects
treatments.context_specific_role: Component of all-oral MDR-TB regimens (BPaL, BPaLM); not used in drug-susceptible disease

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empiric hydrocortisone is life-saving in suspected adrenal crisis; should not be delayed for cosyntropin testing in shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone for refractory hypotension with hyponatremia in disseminated TB; rifampin further increases cortisol clearance, raising replacement doses

cd4_above_350.trajectory_modulation: Modestly increased risk; classical pulmonary or extrapulmonary disease

cd4_below_200.trajectory_modulation: Markedly higher risk of disseminated, miliary, and extrapulmonary disease; atypical CXR; TST/IGRA frequently negative; high HLH and IRIS risk

infant_or_under_5.trajectory_modulation: Higher progression to miliary and meningeal disease after primary infection; mortality higher

elderly_over_65.trajectory_modulation: Higher reactivation rate, more atypical presentations, higher DILI risk

uncontrolled.trajectory_modulation: Slower microbiological response; higher recurrence; greater steroid-induced hyperglycemia complicating TBM treatment

bmi_below_18_5.trajectory_modulation: Reduced cell-mediated immunity; higher DILI risk; slower recovery

tnf_alpha_inhibitor.trajectory_modulation: Particularly high risk of reactivation and dissemination; LTBI screening required before initiation

high_dose_glucocorticoids.trajectory_modulation: Atypical presentations, higher dissemination, IGRA/TST may be falsely negative

solid_organ_transplant.trajectory_modulation: High reactivation rate; complex drug interactions between rifampin and calcineurin inhibitors

esrd_or_dialysis.trajectory_modulation: Higher reactivation; need for ethambutol and pyrazinamide dose adjustment; frequently atypical

present.trajectory_modulation: Markedly elevated risk of TB reactivation and dissemination; longer treatment duration recommended

high_burden_country_origin.trajectory_modulation: Higher LTBI prevalence and reactivation risk

active_heavy_use.trajectory_modulation: Higher DILI risk on RIPE; poor adherence; concurrent malnutrition

present.trajectory_modulation: Higher reactivation; cytopenias confound diagnosis and limit linezolid use

pregnant_or_recent_postpartum.trajectory_modulation: Slightly elevated risk of progression in postpartum; pyrazinamide use varies by guideline; streptomycin contraindicated; close DILI monitoring

supportive_care: Airborne isolation in negative-pressure room until pulmonary involvement excluded or sputum smear negative on three consecutive days with clinical improvement on therapy
Public health notification per local statute (TB is a notifiable disease)
Contact tracing for household and close contacts with TST/IGRA and chest imaging
Directly observed therapy (DOT) or video-DOT to support adherence over 6–12 month course

Baseline and serial liver function tests (ALT, AST, bilirubin, ALP) at weeks 2, 4, 8 and as clinically indicated; immediate stop of hepatotoxic agents for symptomatic ALT > 3× ULN or asymptomatic > 5× ULN
Baseline visual acuity and Ishihara color testing at start of ethambutol with monthly reassessment
HIV testing in all patients; if positive, CD4 count, viral load, and timed ART initiation per CD4 (within 2 weeks if CD4 < 50, by 8 weeks otherwise; delayed in TBM)
Hepatitis B and C screening; consider prophylaxis for HBV reactivation if HBsAg positive
Drug-susceptibility testing on all isolates (Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra rapid + culture-based DST)
Pyridoxine 25–50 mg/day with isoniazid (mandatory in HIV, pregnancy, malnutrition, alcohol use, diabetes, renal failure)
Nutritional support including high-calorie high-protein diet and micronutrient repletion (vitamin D, zinc); food insecurity screening and referral
Ophthalmologic dilated fundoscopy looking for choroidal tubercles at presentation

Lumbar puncture in any disseminated TB patient with headache, altered mental status, or atypical neurologic findings — adjunctive dexamethasone for confirmed or strongly suspected TBM with taper over 6–8 weeks
Empiric stress-dose hydrocortisone (200–300 mg/day) in disseminated TB with refractory hypotension and hyponatremia, with subsequent ACTH stimulation testing once stable
Glycemic monitoring and management, particularly during corticosteroid use
Monitoring for paradoxical / IRIS reactions over weeks 2–12 of therapy (do not interrupt anti-TB therapy; consider corticosteroids for severe IRIS)
Drug interaction review (rifampin is a potent CYP3A4 inducer affecting ART, anticoagulants, contraceptives, calcineurin inhibitors, methadone, oral hypoglycemics)
Pharmacy and case-management support for treatment completion, transportation, housing instability

Follow-up sputum cultures monthly during treatment until two consecutive negative cultures; consider prolonged therapy (9–12 months) for TBM, bone/joint TB, or persistent culture positivity at 2 months
Mental health screening and support given the chronicity, isolation requirements, and stigma of TB diagnosis
